title: See Your Own Network
sub: Read every field macOS tells you about interfaces, addresses, routes, neighbours and DNS, and pipe it into variables
goals: Read an ifconfig block field by field and say what each line means
Tell which interface carries your traffic and why, using the routing table
Extract your IP, MAC, gateway, DNS servers and prefix length into shell variables
Recognise utun, awdl, bridge and link-local entries without panicking
List the neighbours on your LAN from the ARP cache and turn them into a CSV

blocks.text: Before you probe the internet, learn what your own Mac already knows about its network. macOS keeps that knowledge in several places that use different vocabulary: the kernel knows *interfaces* and *routes*, the system configuration database knows *services* and *resolvers*, and the Wi-Fi stack knows *radios*. In this chapter you will read each of those views with read-only commands, learn which command answers which question, and finish by building `netinfo.zsh`, a one-screen report, and the first version of `lan-inventory`, a CSV of every device your Mac has recently talked to.

Every command in this chapter only displays information, except the few marked `WARN`. Run them on your own Mac as you read. The `term sim` blocks run against the practice lab's canned network (`192.168.1.0/24`, your Mac is `192.168.1.23`), so their output is fixed; the `term sample` blocks show typical output from a real Mac, and yours will differ in addresses, interface numbers and extra lines.
Four names for the same thing
The first confusion on macOS is vocabulary. One physical Wi-Fi chip has four different names depending on which tool you ask.

blocks.code:
hardware port      device            network service         what uses the name
  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────┐        ┌────────────────┐
  │ Wi-Fi       │──▶│  en0    │───────▶│ "Wi-Fi"        │       networksetup, System Settings
  └─────────────┘   └─────────┘        └────────────────┘
   (the radio)      (BSD name the        (a saved set of
                     kernel uses)         IP/DNS/proxy settings
                                          bound to a port)
   ifconfig, netstat, route, ping -b, tcpdump -i  all want the DEVICE name (en0)
   networksetup -getdnsservers, -setdnsservers    want the SERVICE name (Wi-Fi)

items.text: A **hardware port** is a kind of connection the Mac has: Wi-Fi, Ethernet adapter, Thunderbolt Bridge.

A **device** is the BSD interface name the kernel assigned: `en0`, `en1`, `bridge0`, `lo0`. On a laptop `en0` is usually Wi-Fi, but on a Mac mini with Ethernet or any Mac with a dock it may not be. Never assume; look it up.

A **network service** is a saved configuration (addresses, DNS servers, proxies) attached to a port. System Settings > Network lists services. The **service order** decides which one is preferred when several are connected.
A **location** is a named set of services. Most people only have "Automatic".

blocks.code:
$ networksetup -listallhardwareports
Hardware Port: Wi-Fi
Device: en0
Ethernet Address: f0:18:98:3a:6d:21

Hardware Port: Thunderbolt Bridge
Device: bridge0
Ethernet Address: 36:55:12:ab:cd:01
$ ifconfig -l
lo0 en0 en1

blocks.text: `networksetup -listallhardwareports` is the translator between the port name and the device. `ifconfig -l` lists just the device names the kernel has right now.

blocks.name: networksetup
blocks.sum: Read and change the network services that System Settings shows: addresses, DNS servers, proxies, Wi-Fi power.
blocks.syntax: networksetup -listallhardwareports | -listallnetworkservices | -listnetworkserviceorder | -getinfo service | -getdnsservers service | -setdnsservers service server... | -getairportnetwork device | -setairportpower device on|off

how.text: `networksetup` is the command-line twin of the Network pane in System Settings. It edits the same preferences store, so changes appear in the GUI at once and survive reboots. Read subcommands (`-get*`, `-list*`) need no privileges; write subcommands (`-set*`) ask for an administrator password.

Most subcommands take the **service name** in quotes (`"Wi-Fi"`, `"USB 10/100/1000 LAN"`), not the `en0` device name. The exceptions are the Wi-Fi ones, which take the device. If you are unsure of a service name, list them with `-listallnetworkservices`; a leading `*` on a line means that service is disabled.

flags.d: Every hardware port with its device name (`en0`) and its hardware MAC address.
The names of all services, one per line. Use these names with the other flags.
Services in priority order with their ports. The first connected service wins the default route.
Address assignment, IP, mask, router and MAC of one service.
DNS servers set manually on that service. Prints a sentence instead of an address when DHCP supplies them.
Set DNS servers manually. The word `Empty` instead of a server clears the list and goes back to DHCP-supplied servers.
The search domains appended to short names.
The SSID the Wi-Fi device is joined to.
Turn the Wi-Fi radio off or on; the classic "have you tried turning it off and on".
The hardware MAC address of the port behind a service.

gotchas: The message "There aren't any DNS Servers set on Wi-Fi." does not mean you have no DNS. It means nothing is configured *manually*; the servers came from DHCP. Read the real list with `scutil --dns`.

`-setdnsservers` overrides what DHCP offers on every network that service joins. Setting `1.1.1.1` at home and forgetting it will break your office's internal names later. Undo it with `networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi Empty`.

blocks.text: `networksetup -getairportnetwork en0` prints `Current Wi-Fi Network: HomeNet`. On recent macOS releases the SSID is treated as location data, and the command can report that you are not associated with a network even while you are connected. The Wi-Fi menu, `system_profiler SPAirPortDataType` and `sudo wdutil info` are the fallbacks; they are covered below.
Reading ifconfig

`ifconfig` (interface configuration) asks the kernel for the state of every network interface. It is the oldest tool in this chapter and the one you will use most. Here is the block for a Wi-Fi interface on a typical Mac, annotated.

blocks.code:
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
 │      │                                                       └─ largest payload per frame (bytes)
 │      └─ state flags, hex bitmask first, names of the set bits inside <>
 └─ device name
        options=6460<TSO4,TSO6,CHANNEL_IO,PARTIAL_CSUM,ZEROINVERT_CSUM>   hardware offload features
        ether f0:18:98:3a:6d:21                                            link-layer (MAC) address
        inet6 fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xe   link-local IPv6
        inet 192.168.1.23 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 192.168.1.255      IPv4 address, mask, broadcast
        inet6 2001:db8:1c2:7a00:8f3:5d1e:b7a4:92c1 prefixlen 64 autoconf  global IPv6 (SLAAC)
        nd6 options=201<PERFORMNUD,DAD>                                    IPv6 neighbour discovery
        media: autoselect                                                   negotiated link type
        status: active                                                      is there a link?

head: Field
What it tells you
rows: The interface state as a bit mask. `UP` is administratively enabled, `RUNNING` means the driver reports a working link, `BROADCAST` and `MULTICAST` list supported delivery modes, `SIMPLEX` means it cannot hear its own transmissions, `SMART` is an old Apple flag for interfaces that manage their own routes. `LOOPBACK` appears on `lo0`, `POINTOPOINT` on tunnels.
Maximum transmission unit, see [Networks](#networks). Tunnels often show smaller values such as 1380 because they add headers.
Offload features the hardware performs for the kernel (checksums, segmentation). You can ignore these.
The MAC address this interface uses. With Private Wi-Fi Address enabled, it is a per-network random address and differs from the factory address that `networksetup -listallhardwareports` prints.
An IPv4 address, followed by `netmask` in **hexadecimal** (`0xffffff00` is `255.255.255.0`, a /24) and, for broadcast-capable links, `broadcast`.

The IPv6 link-local address, valid only on this link. The `%en0` suffix is the **zone**: which link, since every interface has an `fe80::/10` address. `scopeid 0xe` is the same zone as a number: interface index 14.

A global address. `autoconf` means it was built from a router advertisement (SLAAC); `temporary` marks a short-lived privacy address; `deprecated` means it still works for existing connections but will not be chosen for new ones.
`PERFORMNUD` (neighbour unreachability detection) and `DAD` (duplicate address detection) are normal.
`autoselect` on Wi-Fi. On Ethernet you see the negotiated speed, for example `autoselect (1000baseT <full-duplex>)`.
`active` means link up, `inactive` means no link (cable out, Wi-Fi off).

blocks.text: The `secured` word after a link-local address marks an address generated for Secure Neighbor Discovery rather than derived directly from the MAC. You will see it on most Macs and can ignore it.
Which interface is which
A modern Mac lists a dozen interfaces. Most are not your connection to the internet.

head: Name
What it is
Do you care?
rows: Loopback. `127.0.0.1` and `::1`. Traffic to yourself never leaves the kernel.
Usually Wi-Fi on a laptop, or the built-in Ethernet on a desktop
More ports: Ethernet adapters, Thunderbolt bridge members, a second radio, USB tethering. Often `status: inactive`
Software bridge, for Thunderbolt Bridge or Internet Sharing
User-space tunnels: VPN clients, iCloud Private Relay, Tailscale, WireGuard. Point-to-point, small MTU
Yes, when a VPN is running
Apple Wireless Direct Link, used by AirDrop, AirPlay and Sidecar. IPv6 link-local only
Appears when the Mac acts as a Wi-Fi access point (Internet Sharing)

blocks.text: A `utun` ("user tunnel") interface lets a *user-space program* act as a network device: the kernel hands it IP packets, the program encrypts or relays them, and sends the result out on a real interface. macOS itself creates several for system features, so `utun0` to `utun3` existing with only an IPv6 link-local address is normal and does not mean a VPN is running. A VPN adds one with an IPv4 address, like `utun4: inet 10.8.0.6 --> 10.8.0.6`.

blocks.name: ifconfig
blocks.sum: Show or change the configuration of network interfaces: addresses, masks, MAC, MTU, link state.

how.text: `ifconfig` queries the kernel's interface list through ioctl system calls and formats the result. Without arguments it prints every interface, which on a modern Mac is long. With a device name it prints one. With an address family (`inet` or `inet6`) it prints only those address lines.

The same command can change settings (`ifconfig en0 mtu 1400`, `ifconfig en0 down`, `ifconfig en0 alias ...`), but changes made this way are lost on reboot and fight with the system configuration daemon, which will undo them without notice. For permanent changes use `networksetup`.

flags.d: Show all interfaces (the default when no name is given).
Print only the interface names on one line. Combine with `-u` for only those that are up, `-d` for only those that are down.
With `-l`: only interfaces that are up.
Verbose: extra detail such as link quality and rate information.
Restrict output to IPv4 or IPv6 address lines.

examples.desc: Show your Wi-Fi interface
Just the IPv4 line

anat.exp: address family filter: IPv4 lines only

examples.desc: Print the IPv4 address of one interface
List every interface that has an IPv4 address
Show the MAC address of an interface

gotchas: The netmask is hex. `0xffffff00` is /24, `0xfffffe00` is /23, `0xffff0000` is /16. A section below turns hex into a prefix length with `awk`.
There is no `ifconfig` output in `ip addr` style. If a tutorial says `ip a` or `ip route`, it is for Linux; macOS has no `ip` command.

blocks.code:
$ ifconfig en0
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	options=6460<TSO4,TSO6,CHANNEL_IO,PARTIAL_CSUM,ZEROINVERT_CSUM>
	ether f0:18:98:3a:6d:21
	inet6 fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xe
	inet 192.168.1.23 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 192.168.1.255
	nd6 options=201<PERFORMNUD,DAD>
	media: autoselect
	status: active
$ ifconfig | awk '/^[a-z0-9]+:/ {gsub(":","",$1); i=$1} /inet / {print i, $2}'
lo0 127.0.0.1
en0 192.168.1.23

blocks.text: The second command is your first real **pipeline over `ifconfig`**. Read it as a small program: when a line starts with a name and a colon, remember that name in `i`; when a line contains `inet `, print the remembered name and the address. Interface blocks are indented, so the name line and the address line are separate; `awk` carries the name down by remembering it. That "remember the header, act on the detail" pattern appears in almost every parse of a multi-line macOS report.

blocks.title: Walking an ifconfig block with awk

tokens.exp: on lines that start with a name and colon: strip the colon, save the name in i
on lines containing "inet " (with a space, so inet6 is skipped): print the saved name and field 2, the address

blocks.text: Privacy MACs and why yours changes

Current macOS releases can use a **private Wi-Fi address**: a random MAC address per network, instead of the factory-burned one. You see this when `ifconfig en0` shows an `ether` value that does not match the one in `networksetup -listallhardwareports`. It matters in three places: DHCP reservations on your router (the reservation must use the private MAC), MAC filtering, and every `arp` table on the network, which shows the private address.

Depending on your settings and OS version, the private address can be fixed per network or rotate periodically. System Settings > Wi-Fi > Details for the network shows the Private Wi-Fi Address option. Turning it off for your own home network gives a stable MAC that is easier to reserve.
What DHCP gave you: ipconfig

`ifconfig` shows the state. `ipconfig` shows the *negotiation* that produced it. On macOS `ipconfig` is a different program from the Windows one of the same name: it is the client for the system's DHCP and IPv6 configuration agent, and it can show you the exact DHCP reply (the ACK packet) that your router sent.

blocks.name: ipconfig
blocks.sum: Query and control the DHCP and IPv6 configuration of an interface on macOS.
blocks.syntax: ipconfig getifaddr interface | getsummary interface | getpacket interface | getoption interface option | set interface DHCP | waitall

how.text: macOS runs a configuration agent that performs DHCP (the DORA exchange from [Networks](#networks): Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and keeps the lease. `ipconfig` talks to that agent. `getifaddr` prints just the IPv4 address, which makes it the cleanest way to get your IP into a script. `getpacket` prints the last DHCP ACK decoded, including the options the router handed out: subnet mask, router, DNS servers, lease time.

`set interface DHCP` restarts the DHCP exchange on that interface. It needs `sudo` and briefly drops your IPv4 address, so it is the right repair for a stale or 169.254 address, not something to run casually.

flags.d: Print the interface's IPv4 address; exit status 1 and no output if it has none.
A readable dump of the interface's configuration state, including DHCP and, on Wi-Fi, SSID information (which recent releases may redact).
The last DHCP reply, decoded, with every option.
One DHCP option by name, for example `domain_name_server` or `router`.
Renew the lease from scratch (needs `sudo`).

gotchas: `getifaddr` on an interface with no IPv4 address prints nothing and returns 1. In a script, test with `ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr en0) || ...` rather than assuming the variable has a value.
Lease time in `getpacket` is hexadecimal seconds: `0x15180` is 86400 s, 24 hours.

blocks.title: Do not run `ipconfig set` just to look

blocks.text: `sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP` drops and re-requests your lease. If you are connected over SSH or doing a screen share on that interface, your session dies with it. Try it when you are sitting at the machine and can reconnect.
Where your packets go: the routing table

A packet to an address outside your subnet needs a next hop, and the kernel picks it from the **routing table**. [Addressing](#addressing) taught the rule (longest prefix wins); now you read the real table.

blocks.code:
$ netstat -rn -f inet
Routing tables

Internet:
Destination        Gateway            Flags               Netif Expire
default            192.168.1.1        UGScg                 en0
10.8.0.1           10.8.0.6           UH                  utun4
127                127.0.0.1          UCS                   lo0
127.0.0.1          127.0.0.1          UH                    lo0
169.254            link#14            UCS                   en0      !
192.168.1          link#14            UCS                   en0      !
192.168.1.1/32     link#14            UCS                   en0      !
192.168.1.1        a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9   UHLWIir               en0   1198
192.168.1.23/32    link#14            UCS                   en0      !
192.168.1.255      ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff  UHLWbI                en0      !
224.0.0/4          link#14            UmCS                  en0      !
255.255.255.255/32 link#14            UCS                   en0      !

blocks.text: How to read it:

items.text: **default** is the route of last resort: anything that matches nothing more specific goes to `192.168.1.1` out of `en0`. The `G` flag means "via a gateway".

**192.168.1** (shorthand for `192.168.1.0/24`) is the connected subnet. The gateway column says `link#14`, meaning "deliver directly on link 14, no router": the kernel will ARP for the destination. Link 14 is the interface index, the same number as `scopeid 0xe` in `ifconfig`.
**192.168.1.1** has a real MAC address as its "gateway". That is a *host route* filled in by ARP, and `1198` is the seconds until the entry expires.
**169.254** is the link-local range reserved for self-assigned addresses; **224.0.0/4** is multicast; **255.255.255.255** is the limited broadcast.
**10.8.0.1 via utun4** is a VPN tunnel's peer. Anything for `10.8.0.0/24` would also take that tunnel if the VPN adds the route.

head: Flag
Meaning
rows: Uses a gateway (next hop is another router)
Host route: the destination is a single address
Static: added by configuration, not learned from a routing protocol
Cloning: the route spawns host routes on demand, which is how ARP entries are created
Protocol cloning: the protocol (ARP for IPv4) creates host routes from this route on demand
The gateway field holds a link-layer (MAC) address
Was cloned (the route was created from a cloning route)
Global: the destination is on the global internet (a routing policy hint)
Reject: packets to this destination are refused with an error
Blackhole: packets to this destination are silently dropped

blocks.title: Which interface wins the default route?

blocks.text: More than one service can be connected at once (Wi-Fi and Ethernet, or a VPN). macOS picks the **primary** service by service order, and sets the default route through it. `networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder` shows the order, and `scutil --nwi` ("network wide information") shows which interface is currently primary for IPv4 and IPv6. When a full-tunnel VPN connects, it replaces the default route so that all traffic goes through the tunnel; split-tunnel VPNs add specific routes instead.

blocks.name: route
blocks.sum: Ask the kernel how it would send a packet to a given destination, and (with root) edit the routing table.
blocks.syntax: route [-n] get destination | monitor | flush | add ... | delete ...

how.text: `route -n get DEST` is the most useful read-only form: it does a routing lookup *for one destination* and prints the winning route with its gateway, outgoing interface, flags and MTU. It is the direct answer to "where would a packet to this address actually go?" because it applies longest-prefix match exactly as the kernel does. `-n` skips name lookups.

`route -n monitor` prints a line each time the routing table changes (Wi-Fi roaming, VPN connect, DHCP renew), which is a good live view while you reproduce a problem. `add`, `delete` and `flush` change the live table and need `sudo`; the changes vanish at reboot.

flags.d: Numeric output; do not try to resolve names.
Look up the route for `dest`. `default` or any IP works.
Stream routing-table changes until you press Ctrl-C.
Delete all gateway routes (needs `sudo`; breaks connectivity until DHCP rebuilds them).

blocks.name: netstat
blocks.sum: Show the routing table, interface counters, protocol statistics or open sockets.

how.text: `netstat` is four tools sharing one name; the flags pick which. `-r` prints the routing table (`-n` keeps it numeric). `-i` prints a per-interface table of packets, errors and collisions since boot. `-s` prints per-protocol statistics (TCP retransmissions, ICMP counts, IP fragments). `-a` prints sockets, covered in [Ports and services](#ports).
The interface counters are the quickest way to spot a physical problem: a growing `Ierrs` or `Oerrs` column on `en0` points at a bad cable, interference or a driver problem, not at the internet.

gotchas: A host with Wi-Fi and a VPN has more than one `default` line. The first (the one the kernel uses) is the top one; the others carry interface scope flags like `I`.

Column positions in `netstat -i` shift between rows: the `lo0` and tunnel rows have no MAC column, so every number moves one field left. That is why the pipe example tests that field 4 contains a colon before trusting fields 6 and 8.

blocks.name: scutil
blocks.sum: Query the System Configuration database: DNS resolvers, primary interface, proxies, computer names.

how.text: macOS stores its live network state in a database managed by `configd`, the system configuration daemon. DHCP, VPN clients and System Settings all write to it; the resolver, the routing daemon and every app that asks "am I online?" read from it. `scutil` is the command-line window into that database.

Three read forms matter. `--dns` prints **every resolver configuration** (plural: macOS supports per-domain and per-interface resolvers, which `/etc/resolv.conf` cannot express). `--nwi` prints the network-wide view: which interface is primary for IPv4 and IPv6 and whether each is reachable. `--proxy` shows proxy settings that browsers and `curl` may be silently using.

blocks.text: Neighbours: the ARP and NDP caches

Before your Mac sends a frame to another machine on the same subnet, it needs that machine's MAC address. It asks with ARP ("who has 192.168.1.50?"), stores the answer (for up to 20 minutes by default on macOS), and reuses it. That **ARP cache** is a free inventory of everything your Mac has talked to recently, which is why the project below uses it.

blocks.name: arp
blocks.sum: Show or edit the IPv4 neighbour cache that maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local link.
blocks.syntax: arp [-n] -a | arp host | sudo arp -d host | sudo arp -d -a

how.text: `arp -a` dumps the cache: each line is a name (or `?` if reverse lookup found none), the IP in parentheses, the MAC after `at`, the interface and flags. Without `-n` it tries a reverse-DNS lookup for every address, which is slow when DNS is slow. `-n` skips it.

Entries age out after a while (20 minutes by default on macOS). A host you have not contacted recently simply is not there, so the cache is a list of *recent* neighbours, not all devices. Sending traffic to a host (a `ping`) refreshes or creates its entry. An entry reading `(incomplete)` means ARP asked and nobody answered: the host is down, not on this subnet, or filtering.

flags.d: Show all entries.
Numeric: do not resolve names.
Delete an entry (needs `sudo`). Useful when a device changed its MAC.
Delete all entries (needs `sudo`).
Limit to one interface.

examples.desc: Show every neighbour without name lookups
examples.out:
? (192.168.1.1) at a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
? (192.168.1.50) at dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]
? (192.168.1.255) at ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff on en0 ifscope [ethernet]

anat.exp: hostname, or ? when none was found
the interface it was learned on

examples.desc: Neighbour IPs only, sorted numerically by last octet
examples.code: arp -an | grep -v incomplete | awk '{gsub(/[()]/,"",$2); print $2}' | sort -t. -k4 -n

examples.desc: IP and MAC pairs

gotchas: macOS prints MAC octets **without leading zeros**: `a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9` and `0:11:32:aa:3:5d`. If you compare MACs from `arp` with MACs from a router page or `ifconfig`, pad each octet to two digits first, or the strings will not match.
The cache includes the broadcast address (`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`) and sometimes multicast entries. Filter them out when you count devices.

blocks.text: IPv6 has no ARP. Its neighbour discovery is part of ICMPv6, and the cache is read with `ndp`.

blocks.name: ndp
blocks.sum: Show the IPv6 neighbour cache and the routers your Mac learned from router advertisements.

how.text: `ndp` is the IPv6 counterpart of `arp`. `-an` lists neighbours (IPv6 address, MAC, interface, state), `-rn` lists default routers learned from router advertisements, and `-pn` lists advertised prefixes. The state column shows neighbour-reachability: `R` reachable, `S` stale (not confirmed lately but still usable), `D` delay, `P` probe.

flags.d: Show all neighbour entries.
Numeric output.
Show the default router list.
Show the prefix list.

examples.desc: List IPv6 neighbours
examples.out:
Neighbor                        Linklayer Address  Netif Expire    St Flgs Prbs
fe80::a62b:b0ff:fe5c:1109%en0   a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9    en0 23h54m3s  S  R

blocks.text: Wi-Fi, hardware and live traffic
Three more tools complete the picture. They are descriptive rather than diagnostic, but you will meet their output often.

blocks.name: system_profiler SPNetworkDataType
blocks.sum: Print the Mac's network inventory: every service, its addresses, DNS and proxy settings, and Wi-Fi radio state.

how.text: `system_profiler` is the engine behind "About This Mac > System Report". Each data type is a report about one subsystem. `SPNetworkDataType` lists the network services; `SPAirPortDataType` describes the Wi-Fi card (supported standards, current network, channel, signal, nearby networks); `SPEthernetDataType` covers wired adapters. `-json` makes the output machine-readable, which pairs with `jq`.
The reports can take several seconds because they query hardware. Redirect them to a file when you want to run several parsers over one capture.

flags.d: Output JSON (also `-xml`).
Terse; `full` adds everything.

examples.desc: Wi-Fi details: current channel, PHY mode, signal and noise
Network services as JSON
Signal strength and noise of the current Wi-Fi connection
examples.code: system_profiler SPAirPortDataType | awk '/Current Network Information:/ {f=1} f && /Signal \/ Noise|Channel|PHY Mode|Transmit Rate/ {print; if (++n==4) exit}'

examples.desc: Service names from the JSON report

gotchas: The text layout and field names change between macOS releases, so scripts that grep it need to be re-checked after upgrades. JSON key names are more stable than text positions.
Nearby-network lists and SSIDs can be partly hidden unless Terminal has Location Services permission.

blocks.name: wdutil
blocks.sum: Show Wi-Fi diagnostics: signal, noise, rate, channel, security and AWDL state.
blocks.syntax: sudo wdutil info | sudo wdutil diagnose [-q] [-f dir] | sudo wdutil log

how.text: `wdutil` is Apple's command-line Wireless Diagnostics tool. It replaced the `airport` utility, which was removed in macOS 14.4. `sudo wdutil info` prints a summary with sections for networking, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and AWDL. The Wi-Fi section is the part to read: **RSSI** (signal strength in dBm, closer to 0 is stronger: -50 is excellent, -70 is fair, -80 is poor), **Noise** (background level, about -90 is healthy), their difference the **SNR**, the transmit rate, the PHY mode (`11ac`, `11ax`), the channel with its width and the security mode.
`diagnose` runs a long collection and writes an archive you can inspect or send to support. It needs `sudo`, and some identifying fields (SSID, BSSID, MAC) are shown as `<redacted>`.

flags.d: One-screen summary of network, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and AWDL.
Collect a full diagnostic bundle (slow; `-q` skips the prompts).

examples.desc: Wi-Fi health
examples.out:
WIFI
    Interface Name       : en0
    Power                : On [On]
    Op Mode              : STA
    SSID                 : <redacted>
    RSSI                 : -58 dBm
    CCA                  : 12 %
    Noise                : -93 dBm
    Tx Rate              : 573.5 Mbps
    Security             : WPA2 Personal
    PHY Mode             : 11ax
    Channel              : 5g36/40

examples.desc: SNR in dB from RSSI and noise
examples.code: sudo wdutil info | awk '/RSSI/ {r=$3} /Noise/ {n=$3} END {print r-n, "dB SNR"}'

gotchas: Fields vary with hardware and OS version. Treat the layout as something to eyeball, not a stable API.

blocks.name: nettop
blocks.sum: Live per-process network usage: bytes in and out for each program and connection.

how.text: `nettop` is `top` for the network. It groups traffic by process and, expanded, by connection, and shows bytes in, bytes out and retransmits updating live. It answers the question "which program is using my bandwidth right now?", which `ifconfig` and `netstat` cannot. The interactive display needs a real terminal and uses keys to expand and collapse processes; the logging modes (`-l`, `-L`) print samples as text so you can pipe them.

flags.d: Summarise per process instead of listing every connection.
Only TCP (also `udp`, `route`).
Logging mode in CSV form, n samples, then exit.
Logging mode in plain columns, n samples.
Show raw numbers (bytes) instead of human-readable units.

examples.desc: One sample of total bytes per process
Top 5 processes by bytes received in one sample

gotchas: Column positions in the logging output differ between releases. Run it once, look at the header line, and adjust the `awk` field numbers to match.

blocks.text: Pipelines over network output
Everything above prints text for a human. Your scripts want one value at a time. The trick is the same each time: find the line that contains the value, then pick the field.

head: I want...
Pipeline
Notes
rows: My IPv4 on whatever interface is primary

blocks.code:
$ ifconfig en0 | awk '/netmask/ {print $4}'
0xffffff00
$ ifconfig en0 | awk '/ether/ {print $2}'
f0:18:98:3a:6d:21
$ scutil --dns | awk '/nameserver\[/ {print $3}' | sort -u
192.168.1.1

blocks.text: From a hex mask to a prefix length

`ifconfig` prints the mask as `0xffffff00`. To get `/24`, count the 1 bits. macOS ships a version of `awk` that has no hex-parsing function (`strtonum` is a GNU extension), so do it digit by digit: each hex digit is four bits, and a loop that halves the digit and counts the remainders gives the number of set bits.

blocks.title: Counting the set bits of a hex digit

tokens.exp: look up the digit's value, 0 to 15
repeat until the digit is used up
add the lowest bit (1 or 0) to the running count
shift the digit right by one bit

blocks.text: Run it with `0xfffffe00` (a /23) and `0xfffff800` (a /21). Reading that loop is a good exercise in what a mask is: the number of leading 1 bits.
The one-line "who am I on the network"
Combine the pieces and you have the report every troubleshooting session starts with. Break it into variables first, so each piece can be tested:

blocks.code:
iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr "$iface")
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
print "$iface  $ip  via $gw"

blocks.text: If you are offline, `iface` is empty and the next line misbehaves. A script must check for that, which is why the project below begins with a guard. The `myvalues` widget on this page can read the same facts: paste the output of the commands it suggests and it fills in `{{iface}}`, `{{myip}}`, `{{gateway}}`, `{{dns}}` and `{{subnet}}` across the whole book.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Using `en0` blindly.** On a Mac mini or a laptop on a dock, `en0` may be Ethernet and Wi-Fi may be `en1`. Derive the interface from the default route, as above.
**Reading `inet` when you meant `inet6`.** `grep inet` matches both. Use `/inet /` with the trailing space, or `ifconfig en0 inet`.
**Trusting `networksetup -getdnsservers`.** It shows manual settings only. `scutil --dns` shows what the resolver really uses.
**Treating `169.254.x.x` as an address.** It means DHCP failed and the Mac assigned itself a link-local address. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot).
**Comparing MAC strings from different tools.** `arp` drops leading zeros, `ifconfig` keeps them, and routers may print upper case. Normalise first.
**Forgetting that the cache is a cache.** A device missing from `arp -a` may be alive and simply not contacted lately.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Label a real ifconfig block

task.text: Read this sample and answer the questions. It is from a MacBook on Wi-Fi with a VPN client running.

task.code:
$ ifconfig
lo0: flags=8049<UP,LOOPBACK,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 16384
	inet 127.0.0.1 netmask 0xff000000
	inet6 ::1 prefixlen 128
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 3e:5a:c0:12:9b:77
	inet6 fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xe
	inet 10.0.20.134 netmask 0xfffffc00 broadcast 10.0.23.255
	media: autoselect
	status: active
en1: flags=8822<BROADCAST,SMART,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 6a:11:22:33:44:55
	media: autoselect (none)
	status: inactive
awdl0: flags=8943<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,PROMISC,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 8e:77:1f:aa:c4:02
	inet6 fe80::8c77:1fff:feaa:c402%awdl0 prefixlen 64 scopeid 0x10
utun4: flags=8051<UP,POINTOPOINT,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 1380
	inet 172.16.55.9 --> 172.16.55.9 netmask 0xffffffff

items.text: Which interface is the Wi-Fi connection, and how do you know it has a link?
What is the prefix length of the `en0` subnet, and what is the subnet's broadcast address?
Is `en1` in use?
What does `utun4` tell you?
Does the `ether` on `en0` look like a factory address?

hints: A mask of `0xfffffc00` has 22 one-bits (ff ff fc = 8+8+6). The broadcast address is shown for you.
A locally administered MAC has bit 1 of the first octet set: the first octet's second hex digit is 2, 6, A or E.
blocks.solution:
1. `en0`: `status: active` and the `RUNNING` flag, with an IPv4 address.
2. `0xfffffc00` is /22, so the subnet is `10.0.20.0/22` (10.0.20.0 to 10.0.23.255) and broadcast is `10.0.23.255`.
3. No: `status: inactive`, no addresses, and no `RUNNING` flag.
4. A VPN or tunnel client is connected: `POINTOPOINT`, a small MTU (1380) and an IPv4 address. The "-->" form shows a point-to-point link with no real subnet.
5. No. The first octet `3e` has the "locally administered" bit set (3e in binary ends in ...10), so this is a random, private Wi-Fi address.

why.text: Reading interface blocks quickly means checking four things in order: flags and status (is the link up), the `inet` line (what address and mask), the interface type from its name (physical, tunnel or system), and the MAC (factory or private). The same habit works on any Mac.

blocks.title: Three facts from three commands

task.text: Without typing any address by hand, print on three lines: your default interface, your IPv4 address on that interface, and your gateway. Store each in a variable first, then print them with `print -l` (one argument per line).

hints: The interface comes from `route -n get default`; feed it to `ipconfig getifaddr`.
Use `$( )` to capture each value into `iface`, `ip` and `gw`.
blocks.solution:
iface=$(route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface)
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
print -l "interface: $iface" "address: $ip" "gateway: $gw"

why.text: Each fact has a command that prints it in a fixed place; `awk` selects the line and the field, and `$( )` turns the output into a value. Nothing is hard-coded, so the same lines work on Wi-Fi, Ethernet or a dock.

blocks.title: Hex mask to prefix

task.text: Use the `awk` loop from this chapter on a mask of your own. First run it on `0xffffff00`, then replace it with the real netmask from your Mac by putting an `ifconfig` pipeline in front of it, so it prints something like `192.168.1.23/24`.

hints: Print the address with `$2` and the mask with `$4` from the line containing `inet `.
Keep the mask in an awk variable (`m=$4`) before reusing `$1`-style fields inside the loop.

why.text: The mask is only data until you count its leading ones. The loop converts each hex digit to its bit count; `a` remembers the address so the final `print` can join both pieces.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose

task.text: Run `ipconfig getifaddr en9` (an interface that does not exist) and then `echo $?`. Then write a version of your "my IP" command that never names an interface and still works, and prove it by running it. Finally explain, in one sentence, why a script that did `ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr en9)` and then `ping -c 1 $ip` would behave badly.

hints: A missing interface prints nothing, so `$ip` is empty.
`ping -c 1` with an empty argument prints a usage message instead of probing anything.
blocks.solution:
ipconfig getifaddr en9; echo $?
ipconfig getifaddr $(route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')

why.text: The command fails silently with status 1 and no output, so an unchecked variable is empty and the next command runs with a missing argument. Deriving the interface from the default route removes the wrong guess, and checking `$?` or `[[ -n $ip ]]` catches the failure.

blocks.title: Neighbours as numbers

task.text: Using only `arp -an` and the practice terminal or your Mac, print the IP addresses of your neighbours sorted by their last octet, leaving out the broadcast address (the one ending in `.255`) and any `(incomplete)` entries.

hints: `sort -t. -k4 -n` sorts numerically on the fourth dot-separated field.
blocks.solution: arp -an | grep -v incomplete | awk '{gsub(/[()]/,"",$2); print $2}' | grep -v '\.255$' | sort -t. -k4 -n

why.text: `arp` prints each IP inside parentheses; `gsub` strips them, `grep -v` removes the lines you do not want, and `sort` with a field separator and key compares the last octet as a number rather than as text.

blocks.title: Which way does this packet go?

task.text: A Mac has this IPv4 routing table: `default via 192.168.1.1 en0`, `192.168.1.0/24 link en0`, `10.8.0.0/24 via 10.8.0.6 utun4`, `10.0.0.0/8 via 10.8.0.6 utun4`. For each destination say which route and interface is used: `192.168.1.77`, `10.8.0.50`, `10.20.30.40`, `93.184.216.34`. Then say which command would confirm your answer for one of them.

hints: The most specific (longest) matching prefix wins.
blocks.solution:
192.168.1.77: the `/24` connected route, out `en0`, delivered directly (ARP for the host).
10.8.0.50: the `10.8.0.0/24` route, via `10.8.0.6` on `utun4` (a /24 is longer than the /8).
10.20.30.40: only `10.0.0.0/8` matches, so via `10.8.0.6` on `utun4`.
93.184.216.34: nothing specific matches, so the default route: `192.168.1.1` on `en0`.
Confirm with `route -n get 10.20.30.40`.

why.text: The kernel compares the destination with every route and picks the longest prefix. `route -n get` applies the same logic and tells you the winning interface and gateway.

questions.why: The mask is written in hex. `ff` is 255, so four octets of `ff ff ff 00` are 255.255.255.0, which is 24 one-bits.

questions.q: Which command answers "which interface would carry traffic to 93.184.216.34"?
questions.why: `route -n get` does a routing lookup for one destination and prints the interface and gateway the kernel would use.

questions.q: `networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi` prints "There aren't any DNS Servers set on Wi-Fi." What is true?

options.text: The Mac has no DNS and cannot resolve names
No DNS servers are set manually; the servers probably came from DHCP
DNS is blocked by the firewall

questions.why: That command shows only manually configured servers. The effective list, including DHCP-supplied servers, is in `scutil --dns`.

options.text: An Apple wireless direct link used for AirDrop and similar features

questions.why: `awdl0` supports AirDrop, AirPlay and Sidecar. It has an IPv6 link-local address only and is not your route to the internet.

questions.q: Which flag in `netstat -rn` means "uses a gateway"?
questions.why: `G` marks routes whose next hop is another router. Connected-subnet routes lack it and show `link#N` as the gateway.

questions.q: Why do MAC addresses from `arp -a` sometimes fail to match ones from your router's page?

options.text: macOS prints octets without leading zeros, and other tools may use upper case
The router uses a different hash

questions.why: `arp` prints `0:11:32:aa:3:5d` for `00:11:32:aa:03:5d`. Pad each octet to two hex digits and lowercase everything before comparing.

blocks.text: You will build two small tools. `netinfo.zsh` prints a clean table of your own network facts. `lan-inventory.zsh` turns the ARP cache into a CSV file. Both grow in later chapters: [Reachability and path](#net-reach) adds timing, [Ports and services](#ports) adds scanning.
Step 1: Collect the facts with a guard
Create `~/lab/netinfo.zsh` (in PyCharm, or with `nano netinfo.zsh`). The first lines refuse to run when you are offline, which prevents every later line from running on empty variables.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# netinfo.zsh - one-screen summary of this Mac's network
setopt pipefail

mask2prefix() {
  print -r -- "$1" | awk '{h=substr($1,3); n=0
    for (i=1; i<=length(h); i++) {
      d = index("0123456789abcdef", substr(h,i,1)) - 1
      while (d > 0) { n += d % 2; d = int(d/2) }
    }
    print n}'
}

iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
if [[ -z $iface ]]; then
  print -u2 "netinfo: no default route; are you connected?"
  exit 1
fi

ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface)
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
mac=$(ifconfig $iface | awk '/ether/ {print $2}')
mask=$(ifconfig $iface | awk '/netmask/ {print $4}')
dns=$(scutil --dns | awk '/nameserver\[[0-9]+\]/ {print $3}' | sort -u | paste -sd, -)
port=$(networksetup -listallhardwareports | awk -v d=$iface '/^Hardware Port/ {p=substr($0,16)} $1=="Device:" && $2==d {print p}')
host=$(scutil --get LocalHostName 2>/dev/null)

blocks.text: Step 2: Print a table
Append this to the end of `netinfo.zsh`. `printf` with `%-12s` pads each label to the same width.

blocks.title: Make the output feed another tool

blocks.text: Add a `-j` flag in your next version that prints the same values as `key=value` lines, so another script can `source` or `grep` them. That is the shape of a useful tool: a human view and a machine view of the same data.
Step 3: Turn the ARP cache into an inventory

`lan-inventory.zsh` starts small. It reads `arp -a`, normalises each MAC (padding the octets, lower case), skips broadcast and incomplete entries, and writes a CSV with a header. Because the cache only holds recent neighbours, the file starts as a list of devices you have already talked to.
Step 4: Fill the cache first

The inventory is only as complete as the cache. Touch every address on your subnet once, then run it again. The sweep itself belongs to the next chapter; for now, ping the gateway and one or two devices you know, and compare the before and after row counts. Where does a device with a `?` name get its name later? That question is answered in [DNS](#dns).

Add a column for the vendor using the first three octets (the OUI, see [Addressing](#addressing)) from a small lookup table of your own. Skip addresses ending in `.255`. Make the script print the count of entries per interface.
Try it in the practice terminal

The practice terminal knows the lab network: your Mac is `192.168.1.23`, the router is `192.168.1.1`, and the Pi, NAS, printer and Home Assistant box answer in the ARP cache. It supports `ifconfig`, `ipconfig`, `route`, `netstat`, `arp`, `scutil` and `networksetup` with canned output, which is enough to rehearse every pipeline in this chapter.
Next
You know what your Mac looks like from the inside. Continue to [Reachability and path](#net-reach), where you send packets out and measure how long they take and where they travel.

terms.def: A network attachment point in the kernel, with a name like en0, that sends and receives packets
The priority list of network services in System Settings; the first connected one carries the default route
The %interface suffix on an IPv6 link-local address that says which link it belongs to
A user-space tunnel interface used by VPNs and system features
Apple Wireless Direct Link, the peer-to-peer radio mode behind AirDrop
A routing-table entry for a single address (flag H)
The route for the subnet an interface sits on; its gateway is shown as link#N
The kernel's table of recent IP-to-MAC mappings on the local link
The time-limited right to use an address handed out by a DHCP server
Received signal strength indicator, in dBm; closer to zero is stronger
Signal-to-noise ratio: signal strength minus noise level, in dB
A per-network random MAC address used instead of the hardware one
